subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Science: The Science of Fermentation and Yeast
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Science strand: fermentation is a process in which microorganisms such as yeast break down sugars and release carbon dioxide and other byproducts, a reaction used in baking bread and producing certain foods.
subjects.resourceLabel: TVO Learn: Grade 6 Science and Technology

quiz.q: What do microorganisms such as yeast break down during fermentation?
options: Rocks
Sugars
Metals
Plastics

quiz.q: What gas is released as a byproduct of fermentation by yeast?
options: Nitrogen
Oxygen
Carbon dioxide
Helium

quiz.q: How does fermentation help bread dough rise?
options: Fermentation has no effect on bread dough at all
Fermentation removes all the air from the dough
Carbon dioxide released during fermentation forms bubbles that expand the dough
Yeast makes the dough colder, causing it to expand

quiz.q: Why might warm temperatures speed up the fermentation process in bread making?
options: Fermentation only occurs at extremely cold temperatures
Yeast is more active and reproduces faster within a certain warm temperature range
Temperature has no effect on how quickly yeast ferments sugar
Warm temperatures always stop yeast from functioning entirely

quiz.q: Why is fermentation considered useful in food production beyond just baking bread?
options: It is also used to produce foods and beverages by breaking down sugars in controlled ways
Fermentation has no practical uses in food production
Fermentation removes all nutritional value from food
Fermentation is only ever used for a single type of food product

subjects.subject: SocialStudies
subjects.title: Social Studies: Government Borrowing and Canadas National Debt
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Social Studies strand: a government sometimes spends more money than it collects in revenue, borrowing funds to cover the difference, and the total amount owed over time is known as the national debt.

quiz.q: What is the national debt?
options: The total value of all goods produced in a country
The total amount of money a government owes after borrowing over time
The amount of money citizens owe to each other
A tax collected only once per year

quiz.q: Why might a government choose to borrow money?
options: It is spending more money than it currently collects in revenue
Borrowing is only done to reduce the amount of government spending
Borrowing money is required even when a government has a surplus
Governments never need to borrow any money

quiz.q: What term describes government spending exceeding its revenue in a single year?
options: A budget surplus
A tax refund
A budget deficit
A trade agreement

quiz.q: Why might a government choose to borrow money to fund large projects, such as building infrastructure, rather than waiting to collect enough revenue first?
options: Borrowing money always eliminates the need to repay any of it
Governments are never permitted to spend money on infrastructure projects
Borrowing allows important projects to begin sooner, with the cost repaid gradually over time
Waiting to collect revenue always allows projects to begin more quickly than borrowing

quiz.q: Why do economists often pay close attention to the size of a countrys national debt compared to the size of its economy?
options: Economists never consider a countrys debt when studying its economy
The size of a national debt has no connection to a countrys economic health
National debt is always considered equally serious regardless of the size of the economy
This comparison helps indicate whether the debt level is manageable or could create future financial challenges

subjects.subject: Language
subjects.title: Language Review: Grammar, Genres, and Oral Presentation Skills
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Language strand review: students revisit split infinitives, satire in literature, writing an advice column, regional dialects, and signposting language in presentations.

quiz.q: What is a split infinitive?
options: A verb with no subject at all
A word that has two opposite meanings
A sentence missing end punctuation
A word placed between to and the base verb of an infinitive

quiz.q: What is satire?
options: A type of poem with no hidden meaning
A story written only for young children
A literary technique that uses humour, irony, or exaggeration to criticize flaws
A factual report with no opinion included

quiz.q: What does an advice column typically respond to?
options: A recipe request
A sports score
A weather report
A readers question or problem

quiz.q: What is a dialect?
options: A completely separate language with no connection to another
A type of punctuation mark
A word with only one possible meaning
A variety of a language spoken in a particular region or group

quiz.q: What is signposting language?
options: A set of hand gestures used instead of words
Language used only in written essays, never in speech
Transitional words and phrases that help an audience follow a presentations structure
Vocabulary that has no connection to organization

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Math Review: Number Systems, Data, and Geometric Patterns
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Math strand review: students revisit binary numbers, pictographs, the golden ratio, the Fibonacci sequence, and area models for probability.

quiz.q: What two digits are used in the binary number system?
options: 0 and 1
1 and 2
0 and 2

quiz.q: What does a pictograph use to represent data?
options: Only numbers with no images
A single unlabelled line
Coloured regions with no key
Repeated pictures or symbols

quiz.q: What is the approximate value of the golden ratio?
options: 0.618 only

quiz.q: How is each term of the Fibonacci sequence calculated?
options: By adding the two terms that come before it
By multiplying the term before it by two
By subtracting one from the term before it
By dividing the previous term by two

quiz.q: What does an area model use to represent probability?
options: A single unlabelled circle with no divisions
The area of a rectangle or square divided into regions
A single point plotted on a number line
A list of numbers with no visual representation

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Science Review: Energy Sources, Cells, and Astronomy
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Science strand review: students revisit hydrogen fuel cells, osmosis and diffusion, cellular respiration, the Doppler effect, and black holes.
subjects.resourceLabel: TVO Learn: Grade 6 Science and Technology

quiz.q: What two gases does a hydrogen fuel cell combine to produce electricity?
options: Nitrogen and oxygen
Carbon dioxide and oxygen
Hydrogen and oxygen
Hydrogen and nitrogen

quiz.q: What is diffusion?
options: A process that only happens outside of living cells
The complete stopping of particle movement
The movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to lower concentration
The movement of particles from low to high concentration only

quiz.q: What does cellular respiration break down to release energy?
options: Water only
Glucose
Carbon dioxide only
Oxygen only

quiz.q: What is the Doppler effect?
options: The complete disappearance of sound over long distances
The change in pitch heard when a sound source moves toward or away from a listener
A change in the volume of a sound with no connection to motion
A change in the colour of light only

quiz.q: What is a black hole?
options: A cloud of gas with no gravitational pull
A type of planet found only in our solar system
A bright star visible from Earth without a telescope
A region of space with gravitational pull so strong that nothing can escape it

subjects.subject: SocialStudies
subjects.title: Social Studies Review: Canadian Leaders, Confederation, and Government Institutions
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Social Studies strand review: students revisit Sir John A. Macdonald, the growth of Confederation, the North-West Rebellion, the cod moratorium, and the role of an ombudsman.

quiz.q: What role did Sir John A. Macdonald hold beginning in 1867?
options: The first mayor of Ottawa
The first premier of Ontario
Canadas first prime minister
Canadas first governor general

quiz.q: How many provinces made up Canada at Confederation in 1867?
options: Seven
Two
Four
Ten

quiz.q: In what year did the North-West Rebellion take place?
In what year did Canada declare a moratorium on cod fishing off Newfoundland?
What does an ombudsman investigate?
options: Weather-related emergencies
Complaints from citizens against government departments or organizations
Only complaints made by government employees
Traffic violations on public roads

subjects.subject: Language
subjects.title: Grammar: Active and Passive Voice
subjects.summary: Grade 4 Language strand: in the active voice, the subject performs the action, such as The dog chased the ball, while in the passive voice, the subject receives the action, such as The ball was chased by the dog.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Grammar: Active and Passive Voice

quiz.q: In the active voice, does the subject perform the action or receive it?
options: A concept unrelated to grammar
Neither perform nor receive it
Receive it
Perform it

quiz.q: In the passive voice, does the subject perform the action or receive it?
options: Receive it
Perform it
Neither perform nor receive it
A concept unrelated to grammar

quiz.q: Which sentence is written in the active voice?
options: A concept unrelated to grammar
The ball chased itself.
The ball was chased by the dog.
The dog chased the ball.

quiz.q: Which sentence is written in the passive voice?
options: A concept unrelated to grammar
The ball was chased by the dog.
The dog is fast.
The dog chased the ball.

quiz.q: Why might a writer choose the active voice over the passive voice?
options: This concept has no connection to writing style
Active voice often sounds clearer and more direct
Passive voice always sounds clearer than active voice
The active voice is never used by writers

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Number Sense: Introduction to Modular Arithmetic (Clock Math)
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Math strand: modular arithmetic finds the remainder after dividing one number by another, often called clock math because a 12-hour clock cycles back to 1 after reaching 12, similar to counting modulo 12.

quiz.q: What does modular arithmetic calculate?
options: The average of a list of numbers
The sum of two numbers
The square root of a number
The remainder after dividing one number by another

quiz.q: What is 14 mod 5?
On a 12-hour clock, what time is 3 hours after 11:00?
Why is a 12-hour clock a useful real-world example of modular arithmetic?
options: Clock times cycle back to 1 after reaching 12, matching how modular arithmetic wraps numbers around after reaching a fixed value
Modular arithmetic has no connection to how time is measured
A 12-hour clock counts upward forever without ever resetting
Clocks never repeat any numbers throughout the day

quiz.q: Why might modular arithmetic be useful in fields such as computer science, beyond telling time?
options: Computers never need to work with repeating or cyclical patterns
It provides a systematic way to work with numbers that cycle or repeat in a fixed pattern, useful for tasks such as scheduling or encoding data
Modular arithmetic removes the need for any other type of calculation
Modular arithmetic can only be used to calculate exact, non-repeating totals

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Science: Crystal Formation and Crystallization
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Science strand: crystallization occurs when a dissolved substance separates from a solution and its particles arrange themselves into a repeating geometric pattern, forming a solid crystal, a process that can be sped up by cooling or evaporating a solution.
subjects.resourceLabel: TVO Learn: Grade 6 Science and Technology

quiz.q: What is crystallization?
options: A process that only occurs inside living cells
The complete disappearance of a dissolved substance
A process in which a dissolved substance separates from a solution and forms a solid with a repeating geometric pattern
A process that turns a solid directly into a gas

quiz.q: What can speed up the crystallization process in a solution?
options: Removing all dissolved substance from the solution
Adding more solvent to the solution
Cooling or evaporating the solution
Keeping the solution at a constant warm temperature indefinitely

quiz.q: What repeating structure do the particles in a crystal typically form?
options: A gaseous cloud with no particles
A liquid structure with no fixed shape
A completely random, unrepeated arrangement
A repeating geometric pattern

quiz.q: Why do crystals often form specific geometric shapes, such as cubes or hexagons?
options: The particles arrange themselves in a repeating pattern determined by how they bond together at a molecular level
Crystals never have any predictable shape at all
Crystal shapes are chosen randomly with no connection to particle arrangement
All crystals form the exact same shape regardless of their particles

quiz.q: Why might scientists grow crystals slowly in a laboratory rather than quickly?
options: The speed of crystallization has no effect on the size of the resulting crystals
Crystals can only form correctly when cooled instantly
Growing crystals slowly always produces smaller, weaker crystals
Slower crystallization generally allows larger, more well formed crystals to develop, since the particles have more time to arrange into an orderly pattern

subjects.subject: SocialStudies
subjects.title: Social Studies: Nellie McClung and the Fight for Womens Suffrage in Canada
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Social Studies strand: Nellie McClung was a Canadian author and activist who campaigned for womens right to vote, helping Manitoba become the first province to grant women suffrage in 1916.

quiz.q: What cause did Nellie McClung campaign for?
options: Free international trade agreements
Womens right to vote
Lower taxes for farmers
The construction of new railways

quiz.q: Which province became the first in Canada to grant women the right to vote, largely due to activists like McClung?
options: Manitoba
British Columbia
Quebec
Ontario

quiz.q: In what year did Manitoba grant women the right to vote?
Why might activists like Nellie McClung have used writing and public speaking to advance their cause?
options: Writing and speaking had no effect on public opinion at the time
Only government officials were permitted to discuss voting laws
Activists were legally required to remain silent about their views
Public writing and speaking could reach and persuade a wide audience, building support for changing unfair laws

quiz.q: Why is the history of the womens suffrage movement in Canada still studied today?
options: The movement had no lasting impact on Canadian law
Voting rights in Canada have never changed since Confederation
It highlights how organized advocacy can lead to meaningful legal change and expanded rights over time
Studying past advocacy movements has no relevance to understanding rights today

subjects.subject: Language
subjects.title: Reading: Understanding Motifs in Literature
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Language strand: a motif is a recurring image, symbol, or idea that appears repeatedly throughout a literary work, helping to reinforce its central themes.

quiz.q: What is a motif?
options: A recurring image, symbol, or idea that appears repeatedly throughout a literary work
A type of punctuation used in dialogue
The title of a book
A single event that happens only once in a story

quiz.q: What is one purpose of a motif in a story?
options: It has no connection to a storys meaning
It replaces the need for a plot
It helps reinforce the storys central themes
It only appears one single time in a story

quiz.q: Which of these could serve as a motif if it appeared repeatedly throughout a novel?
options: The font used in printing
A page number
The books total word count
A particular colour, object, or phrase

quiz.q: Why might an author repeat a specific image, such as a caged bird, throughout a story?
options: A repeated image can never be connected to a storys theme
Authors never repeat images or ideas within a single story
Repetition can draw attention to an idea, such as a feeling of being trapped, and connect it to a larger theme
Repeating an image always confuses readers with no benefit

quiz.q: Why is recognizing motifs useful for a reader analyzing a novels deeper meaning?
options: A novels deeper meaning can only be found in its title
Motifs never reveal anything about an authors intended themes
Recognizing patterns in a text always distracts from its meaning
Noticing patterns that repeat can reveal ideas the author wants to emphasize beyond the surface events of the plot

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Fractions: Subtracting Fractions with Unlike Denominators
subjects.summary: Grade 4 Math strand: to subtract fractions with unlike denominators, students find a common denominator, rewrite each fraction as an equivalent fraction, then subtract the numerators.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Fractions: Subtracting Fractions with Unlike Denominators

quiz.q: What must fractions have before they can be subtracted directly?
options: A common denominator
Different denominators
The same numerator
A common numerator

quiz.q: What is 1/2 - 1/4?
What is 2/3 - 1/6?
What is the first step in subtracting fractions with unlike denominators?
options: Add the fractions
Multiply the numerators
Subtract the denominators
Find a common denominator

quiz.q: Why cant we subtract fraction numerators directly when denominators differ?
options: Subtraction is impossible with fractions
Because the pieces are different sizes until denominators match
Denominators do not matter
Numerators are always equal

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Science: Earths Magnetic Field and How a Compass Works
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Science strand: Earth behaves like a giant magnet with a magnetic field that stretches from pole to pole, and a compass needle aligns itself with this field to point toward magnetic north.
subjects.resourceLabel: TVO Learn: Grade 6 Science and Technology

quiz.q: What does Earth behave like, according to scientists studying magnetism?
options: A giant magnet with a magnetic field
A magnet only at its exact center
An object with no magnetic properties at all
A completely non-magnetic sphere

quiz.q: What does a compass needle align itself with?
options: The nearest large body of water
Earths magnetic field
The position of the sun only
The direction of the wind

quiz.q: Toward what does a compass needle typically point?
options: The nearest mountain
The equator
Magnetic north
The center of Earth

quiz.q: Why has a compass been such a useful navigation tool throughout history?
options: It provides a reliable way to determine direction using Earths magnetic field, even when other landmarks are not visible
A compass only works when landmarks are already clearly visible
Earths magnetic field has no connection to how a compass functions
Compasses have never been useful for navigation

quiz.q: Why might a compass give an inaccurate reading if held too close to a strong magnet or large piece of metal?
options: Nearby metal objects always make a compass more accurate
Compass needles are never affected by nearby magnetic materials
Earths magnetic field becomes stronger near metal objects
A nearby magnetic source can interfere with the compass needles alignment to Earths much weaker magnetic field

subjects.subject: SocialStudies
subjects.title: Social Studies: Equalization Payments Between Canadian Provinces
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Social Studies strand: equalization payments are funds transferred by the federal government to less wealthy provinces so that all provinces can provide reasonably similar levels of public services at reasonably similar levels of taxation.

quiz.q: What are equalization payments?
options: Fees charged to municipalities for road repairs
Funds transferred by the federal government to less wealthy provinces
Loans that provinces must repay to private banks
Taxes collected exclusively from foreign visitors

quiz.q: What is the main goal of the equalization payment system?
options: To help all provinces provide reasonably similar levels of public services
To replace provincial taxes entirely
To fund only one province permanently
To eliminate all provincial governments

quiz.q: Which level of government provides equalization payments to provinces?
options: Foreign governments
Municipal governments
The federal government
Private companies

quiz.q: Why might a country like Canada choose to redistribute funds between provinces of differing wealth?
options: Redistribution can help ensure that residents across the country have access to comparable services such as healthcare and education, regardless of where they live
Redistributing funds always reduces the quality of services in every province
Provinces are never permitted to have differing levels of wealth
Equalization payments have no connection to public services

quiz.q: Why can equalization payments sometimes be a source of political debate between provinces?
options: Every province receives the exact same amount regardless of wealth
All provinces always agree completely on how equalization payments should work
Provinces receiving fewer payments may feel their contributions outweigh what they receive back, while others may depend on the funding to maintain public services
Equalization payments are never discussed in Canadian politics

subjects.subject: Language
subjects.title: Writing: Writing a Speech of Introduction
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Language strand: a speech of introduction presents a guest speaker to an audience by briefly highlighting their background and achievements, building excitement and credibility before they begin speaking.

quiz.q: What does a speech of introduction typically present?
options: A guest speaker to an audience
An unrelated news story
A list of upcoming school events
A detailed weather forecast

quiz.q: What does a speech of introduction usually highlight about the speaker?
options: A detailed weather forecast
An unrelated news story
The introducers own opinions on unrelated topics
Their background and achievements

quiz.q: What is one goal of a speech of introduction?
options: Building excitement and credibility before the speaker begins
Replacing the guest speakers entire presentation
Making the audience forget about the guest speaker
Discouraging the audience from listening further

quiz.q: Why should a speech of introduction remain relatively brief?
options: Length has no effect on how an audience responds to an introduction
A brief introduction always fails to properly welcome a guest speaker
Longer introductions are always more effective than shorter ones
A concise introduction keeps the audiences focus on the guest speaker rather than the person introducing them

quiz.q: Why might including a specific accomplishment or credential in an introduction help the audience?
options: General statements always build more trust than specific details
Credentials have no effect on how an audience perceives a speaker
Specific details can establish why the speaker is worth listening to, building trust and interest before they even begin
Specific details always make an introduction less credible

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Geometry: Surface Area of Rectangular Prisms
subjects.summary: Grade 4 Math strand: the surface area of a rectangular prism is the total area of all six of its faces, found by calculating the area of each face and adding them together.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Geometry: Surface Area of Rectangular Prisms

quiz.q: What is surface area?
options: The space inside a shape
The total area of all the faces of a 3D shape
The distance around a shape
The height of a shape only

quiz.q: How many faces does a rectangular prism have?
options: Six
Three
Four
Eight

quiz.q: To find the surface area of a rectangular prism, you should ___.
options: Add only two of the faces
Find the area of each face and add them together
Ignore the top and bottom faces
Multiply only the length and width once

quiz.q: Why might builders need to know the surface area of a box?
options: To find out how heavy the box is
To know how much material is needed to cover its outside
To find how loud the box is
Surface area has no real use

quiz.q: If a cube has six identical square faces each with an area of 4 square units, what is its total surface area?
options: 16 square units
24 square units
4 square units
20 square units

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: The Digestive System: Where Food Goes
subjects.summary: Grade 1 Science strand: after we eat, food travels through our body from the mouth to the stomach, where our body breaks it down for energy.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: The Digestive System: Where Food Goes

quiz.q: Where does food first enter the digestive system?
options: The heart
The lungs
The mouth
The stomach

quiz.q: After the mouth, food travels down a tube toward the ___.
options: Ears
Stomach
Skin
Brain

quiz.q: Why does the body digest food?
options: To get energy from it
For no reason
To make it heavier
To make it disappear

quiz.q: The stomach helps to ___ food.
options: Colour
Freeze
Break down
Ignore

quiz.q: Which body system is used to process the food we eat?
options: The nervous system
The digestive system
The respiratory system
The skeletal system

worksheet.prompt: Where does food first enter your body?
What body part helps break down food after the mouth?
Why does our body break down food?

subjects.subject: SocialStudies
subjects.title: Social Studies: The White Paper of 1969 and First Nations Opposition
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Social Studies strand: the 1969 White Paper was a federal government policy proposal that would have eliminated the Indian Act and existing treaty rights, but it was withdrawn after strong opposition from First Nations leaders and communities across Canada.

quiz.q: What government document is known as the White Paper of 1969?
options: A federal policy proposal that would have eliminated the Indian Act and existing treaty rights
A treaty signed between Canada and another country
A provincial budget report
A report on Canadian trade with Europe

quiz.q: How did First Nations leaders and communities respond to the White Paper?
options: They were not informed of the proposal
They strongly opposed it
They had no reaction to the proposal at all
They immediately approved it with no concerns

quiz.q: What happened to the White Paper after facing this opposition?
options: It was withdrawn
It was immediately passed into law
It became a permanent part of the constitution unchanged
It was expanded to apply to more countries

quiz.q: Why might First Nations leaders have opposed a policy that removed the Indian Act and treaty rights, even though the Indian Act itself contained many discriminatory provisions?
options: The Indian Act contained no provisions related to land or governance
Treaty rights and existing legal recognition were seen as important protections, and removing them without proper consultation could have eliminated hard-won rights rather than improving them
Removing legal recognition was expected to immediately improve conditions for First Nations peoples
First Nations leaders had no concerns about losing treaty rights

quiz.q: Why is the response to the White Paper considered an important moment in the history of Indigenous political organizing in Canada?
options: The response had no lasting effect on government policy
It demonstrated the impact of unified political action and helped shape future government consultation with Indigenous peoples
The White Paper was never discussed or opposed by any First Nations leaders
Indigenous political organizing began for the first time after this event

subjects.subject: Language
subjects.title: Vocabulary: Malapropisms and Word Confusion
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Language strand: a malapropism occurs when a speaker mistakenly uses a word that sounds similar to the intended word but has a very different, often humorous, meaning.

quiz.q: What is a malapropism?
options: A word with exactly one correct pronunciation
A word that has no other similar-sounding words
The mistaken use of a word that sounds similar to the intended word but has a different meaning
A formal word used only in legal documents

quiz.q: What effect does a malapropism often have on a sentence?
options: It is always used intentionally for formal writing
It always makes the sentence perfectly accurate
It creates an unintended and often humorous meaning
It removes all meaning from a sentence

quiz.q: Which of these phrases contains a malapropism?
options: For all intents and purposes, we should leave now.
We should leave now, for good reason.
For all intensive purposes, we should leave now.
We should leave immediately without hesitation.

quiz.q: Why do malapropisms often occur between words that sound alike?
options: Malapropisms are always planned in advance before speaking
Malapropisms only occur between words with completely different sounds
Similar-sounding words can be easily confused in memory or in quick speech, leading a speaker to substitute the wrong one
Speakers never confuse words that sound similar to each other

quiz.q: Why might authors sometimes use malapropisms intentionally when writing dialogue for a character?
options: Malapropisms never reveal anything about a characters personality
Intentional malapropisms always make dialogue less realistic
Intentional malapropisms can add humour and reveal something about a characters personality or level of confidence
Authors are never permitted to use incorrect word choices in dialogue

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Data Management: Range as a Measure of Spread
subjects.summary: Grade 4 Math strand: the range of a data set is found by subtracting the smallest value from the largest value, showing how spread out the data is.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Data Management: Range as a Measure of Spread

quiz.q: What is the range of a data set?
options: The middle value
The average of all values
The difference between the largest and smallest values
The most common value

quiz.q: What is the range of this data set: 4, 7, 9, 12, 15?
How do you calculate the range?
options: Subtract the smallest value from the largest value
Add all the values together
Multiply the largest and smallest values
Count the number of values

quiz.q: What does a large range suggest about a data set?
options: The data values are spread far apart
The data set has no largest value
All the data values are identical
The data set has no smallest value

quiz.q: What does a small range suggest about a data set?
options: The data cannot be measured
The data values are spread very far apart
The data values are close together
There is no data at all

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Science: Sonar Technology and Mapping the Ocean Floor
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Science strand: sonar uses sound waves to detect objects and measure distances underwater, sending out a pulse of sound and calculating distance based on how long the echo takes to return.
subjects.resourceLabel: TVO Learn: Grade 6 Science and Technology

quiz.q: What does sonar use to detect objects underwater?
options: Visible light only
Sound waves
Radio signals only
Magnetic fields

quiz.q: How does sonar calculate the distance to an object?
options: By measuring how long it takes for an echo to return after a sound pulse is sent out
By measuring the colour of the water
By counting the number of waves on the surface
By measuring the water temperature only

quiz.q: What is one major use of sonar technology?
options: Mapping the ocean floor
Predicting earthquakes on land
Measuring air temperature
Growing crops more efficiently

quiz.q: Why is sonar especially useful for exploring the deep ocean, where light cannot easily reach?
options: Light travels farther through water than sound does
Sonar only works in shallow water near the surface
Sound waves cannot travel through water at all
Sound waves can travel effectively through water even in complete darkness, unlike light, which is quickly absorbed or scattered at depth

quiz.q: Why might a longer time delay between sending a sonar pulse and receiving its echo indicate a greater distance to an object?
options: Sound travels at a fairly consistent speed through water, so a longer delay means the sound had to travel farther before reflecting back
Sonar echoes have no connection to the distance of an object
The speed of sound through water constantly changes with no consistent pattern
A longer delay always means the object is closer to the sonar source

subjects.subject: SocialStudies
subjects.title: Social Studies: The CBC — Canadas Public Broadcaster
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Social Studies strand: the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, or CBC, is a federally funded public broadcaster that provides radio and television programming across the country, including news, entertainment, and content in both English and French.

quiz.q: What does the acronym CBC stand for?
options: The Canadian Business Council
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation
The Canadian Bilingual Congress
The Central Broadcast Committee

quiz.q: How is the CBC primarily funded?
options: It receives no funding of any kind
Through federal government funding
Entirely through private foreign investors
Through provincial lottery revenue only

quiz.q: In which two languages does the CBC provide programming?
options: English and French
Only French
Only English
Spanish and Portuguese

quiz.q: Why might a country choose to fund a public broadcaster like the CBC rather than relying only on privately owned media companies?
options: A publicly funded broadcaster can provide programming that serves the public interest, including news and content that might not always be profitable for private companies
Funding a public broadcaster has no connection to serving public interest
Public broadcasters are never able to provide news programming
Private companies always provide the exact same content as public broadcasters

quiz.q: Why is it important for the CBC to provide programming in both English and French?
options: Canada has two official languages, and offering content in both helps serve and represent both English-speaking and French-speaking communities across the country
The CBC broadcasts only in languages other than English or French
Canada has only one official language, so a second language is unnecessary
Providing content in two languages has no benefit to Canadian communities

subjects.subject: Language
subjects.title: Media Literacy: Analyzing Infographics
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Language strand: an infographic combines images, charts, and brief text to present information visually, and analyzing one critically involves checking the accuracy of its data and considering how its design might influence a viewers interpretation.

quiz.q: What does an infographic combine to present information?
options: Images, charts, and brief text
Only handwritten notes with no images
A list of unrelated numbers with no visuals
Only a single unlabelled photograph

quiz.q: What is one important step when critically analyzing an infographic?
options: Assuming every infographic is entirely accurate
Checking the accuracy of its data
Only reading the title and nothing else
Ignoring all of the images it contains

quiz.q: What might the design of an infographic influence?
options: The number of people who created it
The actual accuracy of the underlying data
A viewers interpretation of the information
The length of the original research study

quiz.q: Why might a poorly designed infographic mislead a viewer even if the underlying data is accurate?
options: A well-designed infographic can never be misleading in any way
Infographic design has no effect on how a viewer interprets information
Choices such as exaggerated chart scales or misleading images can distort how the information is perceived, even without changing the actual numbers
Poor design always makes the underlying data itself inaccurate

quiz.q: Why is it useful to check the original source of the data used in an infographic?
options: Infographics never include data that comes from an outside source
Verifying the source helps confirm that the information is reliable and has not been taken out of context or altered
Checking a source always makes an infographic less trustworthy
The original source of data has no connection to its reliability

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Geometry: Area of Triangles Using a Formula
subjects.summary: Grade 4 Math strand: the area of a triangle is found using the formula base multiplied by height, divided by two, since a triangle is half of a parallelogram with the same base and height.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Geometry: Area of Triangles Using a Formula

quiz.q: What is the formula for finding the area of a triangle?
options: Base multiplied by height multiplied by two
Base plus height
Base multiplied by height
Base multiplied by height, divided by two

quiz.q: What is the area of a triangle with a base of 6 and a height of 4?
What is the area of a triangle with a base of 10 and a height of 5?
Why is the area of a triangle half of base times height?
options: A triangle is half of a parallelogram with the same base and height
A triangle always has zero area
Area formulas are chosen randomly
Triangles have no relationship to parallelograms

quiz.q: Which measurement is needed along with the base to find a triangles area?
options: The height
The perimeter
The number of sides
The colour

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Science: The Ozone Layer and Its Protective Role
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Science strand: the ozone layer is a region high in Earths atmosphere that absorbs most of the suns harmful ultraviolet radiation, protecting living things on the surface below.
subjects.resourceLabel: TVO Learn: Grade 6 Science and Technology

quiz.q: What does the ozone layer absorb?
options: Sound waves travelling through the atmosphere
Most of Earths visible sunlight
Most of the suns harmful ultraviolet radiation
All forms of precipitation

quiz.q: Where is the ozone layer located?
options: At the bottom of the ocean
Inside Earths core
Deep underground
High in Earths atmosphere

quiz.q: What does the ozone layer protect living things from?
options: Harmful ultraviolet radiation from the sun
Ordinary visible sunlight of any kind
All forms of precipitation
Changes in wind speed

quiz.q: Why was the thinning of the ozone layer, once caused by certain chemicals, considered a serious environmental concern?
options: The ozone layer has no connection to protecting life on Earth
A thinner ozone layer allows more harmful ultraviolet radiation to reach Earths surface, increasing risks to living things
A thinner ozone layer has no effect on the amount of radiation reaching Earth
Ultraviolet radiation is completely harmless to all living things

quiz.q: Why is international cooperation, such as agreements to reduce ozone-depleting chemicals, important for protecting the ozone layer?
options: Because the atmosphere circulates globally, chemicals released in one country can affect the ozone layer worldwide, so coordinated action is more effective than isolated efforts
International agreements have no effect on atmospheric chemical levels
Chemicals released in one country never affect the atmosphere anywhere else
The ozone layer can be fully protected by a single country acting alone

subjects.subject: SocialStudies
subjects.title: Social Studies: Canadas Mission in Afghanistan
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Social Studies strand: Canada took part in a multinational military and reconstruction mission in Afghanistan beginning in 2001, contributing troops and aid as part of an international effort following the September 11 attacks.

quiz.q: In what year did Canadas mission in Afghanistan begin?
What kind of mission did Canada take part in Afghanistan?
options: A mission with no international partners
A trade negotiation mission only
A multinational military and reconstruction mission
A purely academic research exchange

quiz.q: What global event was closely connected to the start of the mission in Afghanistan?
options: The fall of the Berlin Wall
The September 11 attacks
The signing of the Treaty of Versailles
The Cuban Missile Crisis

quiz.q: Why might Canada have chosen to contribute troops and aid to a multinational mission rather than acting alone?
options: Acting alone is always easier than working with international partners
Multinational missions never involve sharing responsibilities or resources
Working with international partners can share the responsibilities and resources needed for a large and complex mission
Canada is never permitted to participate in missions with other countries

quiz.q: Why does Canadas involvement in Afghanistan continue to be studied and discussed today?
options: International military commitments never raise questions worth studying
The mission had no lasting effects worth studying
It raises important questions about the goals, costs, and lasting effects of Canadas international military commitments
Canadas involvement in Afghanistan is no longer discussed by historians

subjects.subject: Language
subjects.title: Oral Communication: Non-Verbal Communication and Body Language
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Language strand: non-verbal communication includes body language, facial expressions, gestures, and posture, which can convey meaning and emotion alongside or even instead of spoken words.

quiz.q: What is non-verbal communication?
options: Communication that occurs only over the telephone
Communication that uses only written text
Communication that includes body language, facial expressions, gestures, and posture
Communication that uses only numbers

quiz.q: What can non-verbal communication convey alongside spoken words?
options: Only written text
Meaning and emotion
Nothing beyond the spoken words themselves
Only mathematical data

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of non-verbal communication?
options: Reading a book silently
Typing a text message
Writing an email
Crossing your arms while speaking

quiz.q: Why might a listener pay attention to a speakers body language in addition to their words?
options: A speakers body language has no connection to their true feelings
Body language can reveal additional information about a speakers true feelings or confidence, sometimes clarifying or even contradicting the spoken message
Spoken words always contain all of the information a listener needs
Body language never provides any additional information to a listener

quiz.q: Why is it important for a public speaker to be aware of their own non-verbal communication during a presentation?
options: Being aware of body language always weakens a presentation
Non-verbal communication has no effect on how a presentation is received
A speakers posture and gestures are never noticed by an audience
Their gestures, posture, and expressions can strengthen or undermine the intended message, so being aware of them helps ensure the presentation is received as intended

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Number Sense: Comparing Fractions Decimals and Percents
subjects.summary: Grade 4 Math strand: fractions, decimals, and percents are different ways of representing the same value, and converting between them helps students compare and order numbers.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Number Sense: Comparing Fractions Decimals and Percents

quiz.q: What do fractions, decimals, and percents all represent?
options: Only negative numbers
Completely unrelated concepts
Only whole numbers
Different ways of showing the same value

quiz.q: What is 1/2 written as a decimal?
What is 0.5 written as a percent?
Which is greater, 1/4 or 0.4?
options: They are equal
They cannot be compared

quiz.q: Why is it useful to convert between fractions, decimals, and percents?
options: Fractions and decimals can never be compared
It makes it easier to compare and order different values
Conversion is never useful in math
Percents cannot represent fractions

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Science: Colour Mixing — Additive versus Subtractive Colour
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Science strand: additive colour mixing combines coloured light, such as red, green, and blue, to create new colours including white, while subtractive colour mixing combines pigments, which absorb light and produce new colours by removing wavelengths.
subjects.resourceLabel: TVO Learn: Grade 6 Science and Technology

quiz.q: What does additive colour mixing combine?
options: Magnetic fields of different strengths
Coloured light
Sound waves of different frequencies
Solid pigments only

quiz.q: What three colours of light are commonly combined in additive colour mixing?
options: Orange, purple, and green
Red, green, and blue
Black, white, and gray
Red, yellow, and blue

quiz.q: What does subtractive colour mixing combine?
options: Sound waves of different frequencies
Pigments, which absorb light
Magnetic fields of different strengths
Gases of different densities

quiz.q: Why does combining all three primary colours of light in additive mixing produce white light?
options: Combining coloured light always produces black instead of white
Combining red, green, and blue light at full intensity includes the full range of visible light wavelengths, which the eye perceives as white
Only a single colour of light can ever be produced through mixing
Light mixing has no connection to how colour is perceived

quiz.q: Why do mixing paints, which use subtractive colour mixing, produce darker colours as more colours are combined, unlike mixing light?
options: Each added pigment absorbs more wavelengths of light, so less light is reflected back, making the resulting colour appear darker
Subtractive and additive colour mixing always produce identical results
Pigments reflect every wavelength of light regardless of how many are combined
Adding more paint colours always makes the mixture appear brighter

subjects.subject: SocialStudies
subjects.title: Social Studies: The Indian Act — History and Impact
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Social Studies strand: the Indian Act, first passed in 1876, is federal legislation that has governed many aspects of registered First Nations peoples lives, including status, land, and governance, and it remains a significant and controversial part of Canadian law.

quiz.q: In what year was the Indian Act first passed?
What does the Indian Act govern for registered First Nations peoples?
options: Only matters related to international trade
Only the design of the national flag
Aspects of their lives including status, land, and governance
Only matters related to space exploration

quiz.q: What type of legislation is the Indian Act?
options: An international treaty between two countries
A provincial bylaw only
A municipal parking regulation
Federal legislation

quiz.q: Why is the Indian Act often described as controversial?
options: The legislation was created entirely by First Nations leaders themselves
It has historically imposed significant control over First Nations peoples lives without their full consent, including policies that caused lasting harm
The Indian Act contains no provisions related to governance or land
The Indian Act has never had any effect on First Nations peoples lives

quiz.q: Why do many advocates today call for reform or replacement of the Indian Act?
options: The Indian Act has already been fully replaced with new legislation

They argue that greater self-governance and control over their own affairs would better respect First Nations rights and better reflect modern relationships between First Nations and the Canadian government
Self-governance has no connection to respecting First Nations rights
Advocates believe the Indian Act requires no changes of any kind

subjects.subject: Language
subjects.title: Language Review: The Final Chapter — Grammar, Vocabulary, and Communication Skills
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Language strand review: as the capstone lesson completing the full 187-day Grade 6 curriculum, students revisit the subjunctive mood, motifs in literature, writing a speech of introduction, malapropisms, and analyzing infographics.

quiz.q: What does the subjunctive mood typically express?
options: A question about the past
A command given to a group
A simple statement of fact
A wish, suggestion, or a condition that is not currently true

quiz.q: What is a motif?
options: The title of a book
A type of punctuation used in dialogue
A recurring image, symbol, or idea that appears repeatedly throughout a literary work
A single event that happens only once in a story

quiz.q: What does a speech of introduction typically present?
options: A guest speaker to an audience
A list of upcoming school events
An unrelated news story
A detailed weather forecast

quiz.q: What is a malapropism?
options: A formal word used only in legal documents
A word with exactly one correct pronunciation
A word that has no other similar-sounding words
The mistaken use of a word that sounds similar to the intended word but has a different meaning

quiz.q: What does an infographic combine to present information?
options: Images, charts, and brief text
A list of unrelated numbers with no visuals
Only a single unlabelled photograph
Only handwritten notes with no images

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Math Review: Circles, Fractions, and Time
subjects.summary: Grade 4 Math strand review: students revisit dividing by 10, 100, and 1,000, the circumference of a circle, simplifying fractions, converting units of time, and scatter plots.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Math Review: Circles, Fractions, and Time

quiz.q: What happens to a number when it is divided by 10?
options: The number is multiplied by 10
The decimal point moves one place to the right
The number stays exactly the same
The decimal point moves one place to the left

quiz.q: What is the circumference of a circle?
options: The distance across the middle of the circle
The area inside the circle
The distance around the outer edge of the circle
The number of sides a circle has

quiz.q: What does it mean to simplify a fraction to lowest terms?
options: Changing the fraction into a whole number
Dividing the numerator and denominator by their greatest common factor
Adding one to the numerator only
Multiplying the numerator and denominator by two

quiz.q: How many seconds are in one minute?
What does a scatter plot use to display data?
options: Bars of different heights
Lines connecting single values only
Points plotted on a grid
Slices of a circle

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Science Review: The Final Chapter — Chemistry, Earth Science, and Technology
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Science strand review: as the capstone lesson completing the full 187-day Grade 6 curriculum, students revisit crystallization, Earths magnetic field, the Maillard reaction, sonar technology, and the ozone layer.
subjects.resourceLabel: TVO Learn: Grade 6 Science and Technology

quiz.q: What is crystallization?
options: A process that turns a solid directly into a gas
A process that only occurs inside living cells
A process in which a dissolved substance separates from a solution and forms a solid with a repeating geometric pattern
The complete disappearance of a dissolved substance

quiz.q: What does Earth behave like, according to scientists studying magnetism?
options: An object with no magnetic properties at all
A giant magnet with a magnetic field
A completely non-magnetic sphere
A magnet only at its exact center

quiz.q: What two substances react with each other during the Maillard reaction?
options: Oil and vinegar
Amino acids and sugars
Water and salt
Oxygen and carbon dioxide

quiz.q: What does sonar use to detect objects underwater?
options: Radio signals only
Magnetic fields
Visible light only
Sound waves

quiz.q: What does the ozone layer absorb?
options: Most of Earths visible sunlight
Most of the suns harmful ultraviolet radiation
All forms of precipitation
Sound waves travelling through the atmosphere

subjects.subject: SocialStudies
subjects.title: Social Studies Review: The Final Chapter — Government, Rights, and Canadian History
subjects.summary: Grade 6 Social Studies strand review: as the capstone lesson completing the full 187-day Grade 6 curriculum, students revisit Nellie McClung and womens suffrage, equalization payments, the White Paper of 1969, the CBC, and Canadas mission in Afghanistan.

quiz.q: What cause did Nellie McClung campaign for?
options: Free international trade agreements
Lower taxes for farmers
The construction of new railways
Womens right to vote

quiz.q: What are equalization payments?
options: Loans that provinces must repay to private banks
Taxes collected exclusively from foreign visitors
Funds transferred by the federal government to less wealthy provinces
Fees charged to municipalities for road repairs

quiz.q: What government document is known as the White Paper of 1969?
options: A treaty signed between Canada and another country
A report on Canadian trade with Europe
A federal policy proposal that would have eliminated the Indian Act and existing treaty rights
A provincial budget report

quiz.q: What does the acronym CBC stand for?
options: The Canadian Bilingual Congress
The Canadian Business Council
The Central Broadcast Committee
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation

quiz.q: In what year did Canadas mission in Afghanistan begin?
